question.text: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressive left leg pain for 2 months, which has started to interfere with his sleep. His mother has been giving him ibuprofen at night for “growing pains,” but his symptoms have not improved. One week before the pain started, the patient was hit in the thigh by a baseball, which caused his leg to become red and swollen for several days. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows marked tenderness along the left mid-femur. His gait is normal. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 21,000/mm3 and an ESR of 68 mm/h. An x-ray of the left lower extremity shows multiple lytic lesions in the middle third of the femur, and the surrounding cortex is covered by several layers of new bone. A biopsy of the left femur shows small round blue cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.F: I don't know or cannot answer

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's presentation of progressive leg pain, recent trauma, elevated inflammatory markers (leukocytosis and ESR), lytic lesions on X-ray, and small round blue cells on biopsy strongly suggest Ewing sarcoma. The age of the patient is also consistent with this diagnosis.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Small round blue cells on biopsy are highly suggestive of Ewing sarcoma.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Osteosarcoma is a possibility given the age and bone pain, but the presence of small round blue cells is more characteristic of Ewing sarcoma. Osteochondroma is typically a benign lesion and wouldn't present with such aggressive features. Osteoid osteoma is usually a localized pain and wouldn't cause widespread lytic lesions or elevated inflammatory markers. Therefore, Ewing sarcoma is the most likely diagnosis.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's history of trauma, lytic lesions on x-ray, new bone formation, and small round blue cells in biopsy strongly suggest a malignant bone tumor. Ewing sarcoma is the most common tumor in this age group with these features, especially following trauma. The leukocytosis and elevated ESR support an inflammatory process consistent with tumor activity.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Multiple lytic lesions in the middle third of the femur with new bone formation
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Osteosarcoma (less common in this age group), osteoid osteoma (would not explain leukocytosis), osteochondroma (benign, no leukocytosis), and other benign lesions were considered but ruled out by the combination of findings

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is a 13-year-old with progressive bone pain, systemic inflammation (elevated WBC and ESR), lytic lesions with periosteal reaction on X-ray, and biopsy showing small round blue cells — all highly suggestive of Ewing sarcoma. The history of trauma is irrelevant to the diagnosis, and the absence of fever or systemic illness does not rule it out. Osteosarcoma typically presents with more aggressive bone destruction and a more mature osteoid matrix, while osteochondroma and osteoid osteoma are benign and do not present with systemic inflammation or small round blue cells. The biopsy finding is the most critical diagnostic clue.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Biopsy showing small round blue cells
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Osteosarcoma (less likely due to absence of osteoid matrix and more aggressive presentation), osteochondroma (benign, no systemic signs), osteoid osteoma (typically localized, minimal systemic inflammation), and other sarcomas — all ruled out by age, imaging, and histology.

openbio_8b.clinical_reasoning: The most likely diagnosis for this 13-year-old boy with progressive left leg pain, tenderness along the mid-femur, normal gait, leukocytosis, elevated ESR, multiple lytic lesions in the femur on x-ray, and small round blue cells on biopsy is Ewing sarcoma.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Osteosarcoma (benign vs. malignant histology), osteochondroma (benign, non-infiltrative), and osteoid osteoma (benign, localized to epiphyseal area), but these do not match the biopsy or the pattern of lytic lesions with reactive bone formation seen here.
